title: Codes: BCD, Gray code, ASCII and Unicode; unit-distance codes

items.prompt: Write the decimal number **59** in BCD (binary-coded decimal).
items.explanation: Each decimal digit gets its own four bits: 5 = 0101, 9 = 1001, so 59 = `0101 1001`.

items.prompt: Why would a designer choose BCD over plain binary?
options: Each decimal digit sits in its own four bits, so driving a digit display or doing decimal arithmetic needs no conversion.
BCD uses fewer bits than binary for the same number.
BCD is faster to add than binary.
Binary cannot represent numbers above 9.
items.explanation: BCD wastes six of the sixteen patterns per digit but makes decimal I/O trivial. Calculators and meters use it.

items.prompt: Which of these 4-bit groups are **invalid** in BCD?
items.explanation: BCD only uses 0000 to 1001 (0 to 9). Anything from 1010 (10) upward is invalid.

items.prompt: Convert the binary number `0110` to **Gray code**.
items.explanation: Keep the top bit, then XOR each pair of neighbours: 0, 0⊕1 = 1, 1⊕1 = 0, 1⊕0 = 1, giving `0101`.

items.prompt: Convert the Gray code `1011` back to **binary**.
items.explanation: Keep the top bit, then XOR each new binary bit with the next Gray bit: 1, 1⊕0 = 1, 1⊕1 = 0, 0⊕1 = 1, giving `1101`.

items.prompt: What is the defining property of a Gray code?
options: Consecutive values differ in exactly one bit.
Every value has an even number of 1s.
It is the same as binary but read right to left.
It uses only the digits 0 to 9.
items.explanation: That is why it is also called a unit-distance code.

items.prompt: Where is a unit-distance code such as Gray code especially useful?
options: Rotary position encoders, so a reading taken during a transition is off by at most one step instead of wildly wrong.
Storing text files, so they take less space.
Adding two numbers quickly.
Sending email addresses.
items.explanation: In binary, going from 0111 to 1000 changes four bits; if they do not change at the same instant you might read 1111. In Gray only one bit moves.

items.prompt: What is the ASCII code of the capital letter **A** in decimal?
items.explanation: A is 65 (0x41). The letters run in order, so B is 66 and so on.

items.prompt: In ASCII, how does the code for lowercase `a` relate to uppercase `A`?
options: They differ by exactly one bit (bit 5, value 32): `a` is 97 and `A` is 65.
They are the same code; case is stored separately.
Lowercase codes are the uppercase codes read backwards.
They differ by 1: `a` is 66.
items.explanation: Clearing bit 5 converts to uppercase, which is why case conversion is a single AND.

items.prompt: How do Unicode and ASCII relate?
options: Unicode gives a number to every character in every script; its first 128 codes are exactly ASCII.
They are unrelated encodings for English text.
Unicode is ASCII compressed to 7 bits.
ASCII replaced Unicode in modern systems.
items.explanation: That compatibility is why plain ASCII text is also valid UTF-8.

options: ASCII characters in one byte, everything else in two to four bytes.
Every character in exactly two bytes.
Every character in exactly four bytes.
Only the Latin alphabet; other scripts are not supported.
items.explanation: Variable length keeps English-heavy text small while still reaching every Unicode character, including Twi, Ewe and Hausa letters with diacritics.
